questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a repeated transform produces plausible but wrong values
questions.stem: A colleague asks why converting every measurement from millimetres to centimetres twice produces numbers that look plausible but are wrong. Explain the failure.

answer.exemplar: Each conversion multiplies every value by ten, so applying it a second time multiplies by another ten and leaves every figure in the same ballpark as the originals. Nothing crashes and no value looks absurd, because the arithmetic is uniform across the whole column. The tell is that every number has been scaled by exactly the same factor, and the only way to detect it is to compare a few raw readings against the recorded measurements.

questions.explanation: A repeated conversion scales every value by the same factor, so the column stays plausible and no error is raised. Comparing raw readings with processed values reveals the uniform inflation.
questions.hint: Look for one constant factor across all rows.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a second smoothing pass flattens a survey series
questions.stem: A student asks why applying a smoothing function twice can flatten a survey series that was previously well behaved. Explain.

answer.exemplar: A smoothing function replaces each value with an average of its neighbours, so it already reduces the short-range variation in the series. Running it a second time smooths what the first pass produced, removing further detail, and the result still looks like a smooth line with plausible values. Because the change is gradual rather than sudden, there is no error message and no obviously broken row to point at, so the only way to catch it is to keep the untransformed measurements and compare.

questions.explanation: A second smoothing pass flattens variation the first pass already reduced, and it produces no error because the output stays smooth and plausible. Retaining the untransformed series allows comparison.
questions.hint: Keep the original series to compare against.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a repeated transform from a genuine population change
questions.stem: A colleague asks how to tell a transform applied twice from a genuine change in the population. Explain the diagnostic.

answer.exemplar: A repeated transform multiplies every value by the same fixed factor, so the whole column is scaled together and ratios between rows stay constant, whereas a real change in the population moves the counts unevenly, with some plots up and others down. So the test is to divide the transformed values by the original values and look at the spread of the ratios: a tight cluster around one number indicates a repeated transform, while a scattered set of ratios indicates genuine variation.

questions.explanation: A repeated transform scales every row equally, so old and new values hold a near-constant ratio, while a real population change moves rows unevenly. Examining the spread of ratios separates them.
questions.hint: Ratios that cluster reveal a single factor.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an overwritten conversion is unsafe on a later run
questions.stem: A student asks why a conversion that is safe on one file can corrupt a dataset when applied again later. Explain.

answer.exemplar: A conversion rewrites the values it reads, so after the first pass the column no longer holds what the instrument recorded and there is nothing in the file that says which units it now uses. A later run cannot tell that the conversion has already happened, because the numbers look like ordinary measurements, so it converts them a second time and doubles the error. Keeping the original unit and its label alongside the converted column, or making the script refuse to convert an already-converted column, is what keeps a later run safe.

questions.explanation: A conversion overwrites the evidence of the original unit, so a later script cannot tell the column is converted and converts it again. Preserving the original column makes the second run detectable.
questions.hint: Keep the source column beside the converted one.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain the inconsistency left by transforming only some rows
questions.stem: A colleague asks why applying a transformation to a subset of rows can leave the table internally inconsistent. Explain.

answer.exemplar: If a transformation is applied only to rows matching some condition, then the rows that were transformed and the rows that were not now sit on different scales within the same column, and any summary of that column mixes the two. The table still opens and every number still looks reasonable, so the inconsistency is not visible as an error but only as a strange spread or an odd group average. Recording which rows were transformed, and why, in a flag column carried alongside the data is what keeps the column interpretable later.

questions.explanation: Transforming only some rows leaves the column holding two different scales, so a summary mixes them while nothing errors. A flag column recording which rows were transformed keeps it interpretable.
questions.hint: Note which rows the transformation touched.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a repeated transform arises in a long-running pipeline
questions.stem: A trainee asks why a transform that looks harmless can be applied twice in a long-running pipeline. Explain.

answer.exemplar: A pipeline is often built as a set of scripts that each read a file and write a new one, and the person who wrote the second script may assume the first has already been run on that file, without checking. Over several seasons the scripts are rerun on their own outputs, and a transformation that was assumed to be applied exactly once quietly becomes a repeated application. Recording in each output file which transformations produced it, and having each script assert that its expected input is present, turns the assumption into something the pipeline can check.

questions.explanation: Later scripts often assume an earlier step already ran on the file they read, and reruns turn that assumption into repeated application. Recording the transformations lets each script check its input.
questions.hint: Assert what the input should already contain.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Describe a design that prevents accidental repeated transforms
questions.stem: A colleague asks what design keeps a pipeline from applying a transform twice by accident. Explain.

answer.exemplar: The reliable pattern is to make the transformation idempotent or to make its application detectable. If the transformed column is written to a new field, or the file is written with a record of the transformations applied to it, then a second pass has something to check: the script can see that its expected input has already been converted and either refuse to run or write to a fresh output. A script that converts a column in place leaves no trace of having done so, which is exactly why the second pass goes unnoticed.

questions.explanation: A new output field, or recording the transformations, gives a second pass something to check, so the script refuses to repeat itself. Converting in place leaves no trace of the first pass.
questions.hint: Leave a trace that the step already ran.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the same conversion is safe on one table and not another
questions.stem: A student asks why the same conversion can be harmless on one table and destructive on another. Explain.

answer.exemplar: The danger depends on what the column already holds and on whether the conversion is recorded. On a table of raw measurements in millimetres, converting to centimetres adds a clean, reversible step that is documented in the field book. On a table where a previous run already converted the values and then wrote them back over the originals, the same command has no way to know and converts a converted column a second time. Two tables can hold the same column name and still be in different units, so the safeguard is a recorded unit on every column rather than a rule about the operation.

questions.explanation: The same conversion is safe on raw millimetres and destructive on an already converted column, because the command cannot see what the column holds. Recording the unit per column distinguishes them.
questions.hint: Record the unit on the column, not just the command.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Describe how to establish a repeated transform after the fact
questions.stem: A colleague wants a way to establish, after the fact, whether a survey table suffered a repeated transform. Explain.

answer.exemplar: The evidence has to come from outside the transformed column, because a duplicated transform leaves no mark in the values themselves. Comparing the table against the original instrument file, or against the raw values recorded in the field book, will show a constant ratio between the two for every row, and that constant is the conversion factor applied twice. If the raw file is unavailable, the ratio of the totals before and after, and the sudden presence of values that are implausibly large or small for the quantity, are the next best clues.

questions.explanation: A duplicated transform leaves no mark in the values, so the proof has to come from an independent source such as the raw instrument file, where a constant ratio across rows reveals the double factor.
questions.hint: Look for a constant ratio against raw data.

questions.stem: A survey summary formula was designed for 1,500 readings but now spans 250 cells. How many readings are missing from the computed figure?

questions.hint: Subtract the spanned cells from the intended total.
